result.summary: Pausanias describes Cynætha in Arcadia, with its statue of Zeus at Olympia, its winter festival of Dionysus and its healing well Alyssus. He then turns to the road from Pheneus toward Clitor, which follows a canal dug by Hercules.

scenes.title: Cynætha and its Dionysus festival
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the town of Cynætha, its temple of Dionysus, the bull sacrifice, and the healing well Alyssus.

scenes.title: Road from Pheneus to Clitor
scenes.summary: The road west from Pheneus follows the canal Hercules dug for the Aroanius, reaching Lycuria on the boundary with Clitor.

alias_notes.explanation: The translation spells the Roman emperor Hadrian as Adrian.

notable_quotes.reason: Explains the name Alyssus and the well's cure for mad dog bites.

analysis.text: Pausanias pairs local cult practice with marvels of water, noting the healing well against the deadly Styx.
The statue of Hadrian shows how Roman emperors were honored in Greek towns of the second century AD.

fun_facts.text: The name Alyssus is linked to a Greek word for rabies or madness, reflecting the well's reputed cure.

language_notes.text: Zeus is the name used here; other translations of this book may use Jove. The statue held a thunderbolt in each hand, an unusual image.
A stade was a Greek unit of length, roughly 180–200 metres, so 40 stades is about 7–8 kilometres.
"The god puts it into their mind" means the men believe Dionysus inspires them to choose the bull, so the choice is treated as divine.
Alyssus comes from Greek roots meaning roughly "cure for rabies" or "against madness"; the name explains the well's reputation.
The Styx near Pheneus was said to be deadly water, which Pausanias describes earlier in the Arcadian books, so he contrasts it here with the healing well.
Hercules was said to have dug a canal to channel the Aroanius river and prevent flooding of the Pheneus plain.

context_notes.text: Adrian is the Roman emperor Hadrian (reigned 117–138 AD), who was a generous benefactor of Greek cities and honoured with many statues.
Dionysus was the god of wine, ecstasy and ritual frenzy; bulls were among his sacred animals and forms.
Clitor was a neighbouring Arcadian town to the west of Pheneus, and Lycuria marks the border between their territories.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias speaks as a traveller-guide, ranking sights by how memorable they are, which gives the account a personal, evaluative tone.
The deadly Styx water is set against the healing Cynætha water, balancing two Arcadian springs in a deliberate contrast of harm and cure.
